Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The work is a qualitative study to understand blind and partially sighted people’s needs and challenges in outdoor leisure and to derive a design framework (PLACES) for assistive technologies. It is framed around accessibility, planning, access, and engagement as utilitarian needs, not around creating or adapting an entertainment game. There is no indication of a fun-first or co-designed playful system; instead, the focus is on understanding requirements and barriers to inform future AT design, which aligns best with a mostly utility-first orientation.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The study examines blind and partially sighted people’s real-world leisure use of parks and natural spaces, focusing on planning, accessing, and engaging with these environments. Parks and green spaces are inherently semi-structured leisure settings (paths, facilities, informal activities) rather than rigid games or completely unstructured art/play sessions. No explicit game rules or formal game structures are described; instead, participants engage in typical park leisure, best matching semi-structured play.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: The study is not a game or contest; it is an exploratory survey, interviews, and focus groups about outdoor leisure experiences of blind and partially sighted people. There is no designed element involving probabilistic outcomes or competitive skill; participants simply report experiences and needs. By the given scale, this aligns closest with entirely skill-based (no chance mechanics), though the mapping is imperfect because the study is not a game.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely solo (i.e., solitaire),
        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),
        (3) mix of solo and social affordances (i.e., animal crossing),
        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),
        (5) entirely social (i.e., tag)
reasoning: The study concerns blind and partially sighted people’s leisure experiences in parks, emphasizing both independent engagement with the environment and shared social experiences with companions and the broader BPSP community (e.g., sharing and audio sharing of experiences). This indicates a mix of solo and social affordances rather than purely solo or purely social design.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The paper is not about a game but about a multi-phased leisure experience model (planning, travel/access, on-site activity, recollection). This is closest to a structured sequence of phases, analogous to following a set of steps, so option 2 is the best fit among the given choices.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The study is an online survey plus interviews and a focus group about park-going and technology use by blind and partially sighted people. There is no interactive system or gameplay; participation is not real-time collaborative but consists of answering questions and reflecting on experiences. This aligns best with an entirely asynchronous design.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The study is not a game but an exploration of blind and partially sighted people’s experiences with outdoor leisure in parks, focusing on planning, accessing, engaging, and sharing, including co-planning and contributing with others. The activities described (park visits, shared social experiences, companions, co-planning) are inherently cooperative and oriented toward mutual support rather than competition, so the best-fit category on the given scale is entirely collaborative.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The work is not a game but a framework and qualitative study of blind and partially sighted people’s leisure experiences in parks. There are no roles, turns, or mirrored mechanics between participants; instead, it analyzes one population’s experiences and technology use. By analogy to the symmetry rubric, this maps best to an entirely asymmetrical design (5), as there is no structured reciprocal or mirrored interaction between distinct player roles.
